newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's Mandela to discuss amnesty deadlines.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's Mandela to discuss amnesty deadlines.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela will hear a last-minute plea on Friday to extend the deadline for amnesty applications under a post-apartheid reconciliation programme, his spokesman said on Wednesday.
Apartheid's foes and defenders have until midnight on Saturday to apply for indemnity from prosecution for crimes committed with a political motive.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela would meet a representative of Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Justice Minister Dullah Omar and rightist Freedom Front leader Constand Viljoen.
"He wants to listen to what the Truth Commission and the Freedom Front have to say because they are the ones who have been asking for an extension of the deadline," he said.
"The president is still not persuaded that he should extend the deadline, but it is his prerogative to make up his mind even on Friday," he said.
Tutu told a news conference on Wednesday he hoped the extension would be approved.
"We felt that for the reason of reconciliation we ought to be able to embrace as many people as possible in the process of amnesty," he said.
Tutu said he had also argued "eloquently" that the cut-off date of December 1993 for eligible political crimes should be extended to May 10, 1994, the date of Mandela's inauguration.
Viljoen wants the cut-off date extended to the same date and says the Saturday midnight deadline must also be extended.
In return he has offered to seek amnesty for his plan, never implemented, to deploy 50,000 men in an anti-democracy coup after the first democratic election in April 1994.

So far most veterans of Mandela's African National Congress liberation army and many former soldiers and policemen have rejected the amnesty process. Most former guerrillas argue their war against white rule was just and does not require pardon.
Members of another black guerrilla group, the Azanian People's Liberation Army (APLA), met Tutu on Wednesday and said afterwards they would apply for indemnity from prosecution.

"We are not expecting less that 600 applications from APLA cadres. The commission expects full disclosures and that is what we are going to give them," said former APLA director of operations Happy Mphahlele, now a brigadier in South Africa's unified defence force.
He said APLA members would admit among other things to robberies they had committed to raise funds.
"Self-reliance entailed...repossession and repossession in simple legal terms boils down to robbery. In APLA we had a repossession unit," Mphahlele said.

Tutu has appealed to perpetrators of all human rights offences to come forward by Saturday. "Our political leaders will be squandering an important opportunity for putting the past behind them if they do not come forward and participate in the amnesty process," he said on Monday.
The truth commission's amnesty committee on Tuesday announced the first pardon for a former apartheid security force member.
Policeman Brian Mitchell, serving a 30-year sentence for organising a massacre in which 11 people died in 1988, was freed in a gesture likely to test the limits of reconciliation.
